work_order.understanding:
Issue #74 collects eight leftovers from PR #68 (for #61): seven non-blocking review findings plus one QA finding. Seven of the eight are test and test-helper work; one is a product defect.

The seven review findings are one thing seen from seven sides — a hole in the coverage of #61's fix. Hiding Skip on an exhausted recurrence shipped with a test that cannot fail without it: the reviewer reverted all four scheduleIsSkippable call sites to scheduleIsRecurring and `playwright test schedules.test.ts -g "hides skip"` still passed. Neither e2e fixture is the discriminating input. The one-off fixture's date condition is a plain date, so scheduleIsRecurring was already false for it; the recurring fixture is a plain never-ending monthly, for which getNextDateAfter returns a date under both predicates. The only input where the two disagree is a recurrence whose endMode is after_n_occurrences and whose count is already reached.

The QA finding is separate and pre-existing. SchedulesTable.tsx:225 puts onClick on the whole row body, index.tsx wires onSelect={onEdit}, and onEdit dispatches pushModal, which appends unconditionally, while replaceModal sets modalStack = [modal]. So the second click of a double-click pushes a second identical schedule-edit onto the stack; two live copies mount and one Cancel pops only one.

No decision from a person is outstanding.

On the day-of-month, which the last review rejected v4 over: the ordinal is not a constant. useScheduleEdit.ts:195 seeds start: monthUtils.currentDay(), and util/schedule.ts:181-189 renders a patternless monthly as 'Every month on the {{dateFormatted}}' with the 'do' ordinal. currentDay() is environment-dependent — Playwright pins userAgent to 'playwright' → isPlaywright → '2017-01-01', so the e2e trigger deterministically reads 'the 1st' (a value the repo already asserts at schedules.test.ts:196), while a real browser floats the ordinal. The rule this plan writes instead: the pre-Apply trigger text is captured first and IS the expected text; after Apply the trigger must read exactly that captured string plus a trailing ', once'.
work_order.root_cause: Two independent causes. (1) Coverage, not code: the e2e fixtures are not the input where scheduleIsSkippable and scheduleIsRecurring disagree, and the unit tests call the predicate directly so they pass whatever the call sites do. (2) Stack discipline: the row's onSelect is a modal opener and uses the appending reducer (pushModal) where the replacing one (replaceModal) belongs; onEdit is the only schedule-edit push on the page, so the two were indistinguishable until a user clicked twice.
work_order.approach: Seven edits in dependency order. (1) Add data-testid="recurrence-description" to the picker's trigger Button. (2) Add two methods to the schedule-edit-modal page model: recurrenceDescription() reading the trigger's text, and setRecurrenceEndAfterOccurrences(occurrences?) — neither clicks Apply, because the post-Apply trigger assertion is the caller's. (3) Extend the 'hides skip' e2e test with a third schedule built through the UI (Repeats, end mode 'for', Apply, Add) seeded to start on currentDay(), the only discriminating input; assert its menu lacks Skip while the never-ending monthly keeps Skip; locate rows by payee. (3a) Two trigger-text assertions, in order, neither naming the day: capture preApplyText before opening the popover, assert no ', once' yet, then after Apply assert exactly `${preApplyText}, once`. (4) Delete REACT_INPUT_WARNING_PROBES, the alternatives loop and the trailing page.evaluate; keep the load-bearing guard. (5) Drive the edit path inside the watched window so the fields.name ?? null seed is exercised. (6) Add the double-click test. (7) Rename only the three page-model methods that widened; add editSchedule(row); leave getByRole('menu') unscoped. (8) Restore weeklyOnSaturday verbatim and give scheduleIsSkippable its own factory. (9) onEdit dispatches replaceModal. (10) A release note.

The objection that sank v4 was verified rather than argued with: it is correct, and the fix is mechanical — the ordinal is derived from the app's own pre-Apply text at every one of the ten locations the review named, so no location can disagree with the environment. The rest of v4's claims re-verified this pass: the trigger renders the `value` prop and onSave/Apply is the only write-back; pushModal appends unconditionally while replaceModal sets modalStack = [modal]; the demo budget holds one never-ending monthly and no exhausted recurrence; getRecurringDescription emits 'once' at endOccurrences === 1; weeklyOnSaturday's pre-#68 shape differs from the current one. The single product change is a one-token reducer swap with an existing reducer and a single caller.
evidence: The day-of-month objection, verified at every link: playwright.config.ts:17 sets use.userAgent to the literal 'playwright'; packages/loot-core/src/shared/platform.ts:11-13 exports isPlaywright = navigator.userAgent.includes('playwright'); packages/loot-core/src/shared/months.ts:176-183 currentDay() returns the hardcoded '2017-01-01' when IS_TESTING or Platform.isPlaywright; useScheduleEdit.ts:195 seeds start: monthUtils.currentDay(); packages/desktop-client/src/util/schedule.ts:181-189 renders a patternless monthly as 'Every month on the {{dateFormatted}}' with monthUtils.format(config.start, 'do', locale). work_order.debate_summary:
The previous plan (v4) was rejected with one numbered objection, and it is correct on the source. I reproduced its chain end to end before replanning rather than defending the old text.

The objection: v4 hardcoded the literal day-of-month in the recurring-description string across ten named locations, and the day is 'the 4th' in neither target environment. Playwright pins use.userAgent to the literal 'playwright' (playwright.config.ts:17); platform.ts:11-13 turns that into isPlaywright; months.ts:176-183 makes currentDay() return the hardcoded '2017-01-01'; useScheduleEdit.ts:195 seeds that as the recurrence start; util/schedule.ts:181-189 renders it with the 'do' ordinal. So the e2e trigger deterministically reads 'Every month on the 1st' — a value the repo already asserts at schedules.test.ts:196 — and v4's tests[0].cases[1] and [2] would have failed on the first run, deterministically, every run. In QA's real browser the UA is not 'playwright', currentDay() is the real date, and the ordinal floats; v4 read as verified only because it was authored on a 4th.

What I changed, exactly as the review required. The rule is now stated once and applied at every location: the pre-Apply trigger text is captured and IS the expected text; after Apply the trigger must read exactly that captured string plus a trailing ', once'. The day is whatever the app rendered and the test never names it. Concretely, files[4].change (a) reads `const preApplyText = await exhaustedModal.recurrenceDescription()` before opening the popover and asserts `${preApplyText}, once` after Apply; files[2] adds the recurrenceDescription() page-model method that makes the capture possible. tests[0].cases[1] and [2] are rewritten the same way. AC-1.how_to_verify and AC-2 now tell QA to copy the pre-Apply text and compare against it, explicitly warning the day is whatever today is; AC-2.check states the property ('identical until Apply, then with ", once" appended') rather than a literal. qa_script steps 4-7 are a read-copy-compare chain rather than three readings of 'the 4th'. assumptions[0] no longer asserts 'the 4th'. The e2e suite's pinned date is named once, in files[4].why and tests[0].cases[2], as a property of that environment ('the captured text is "Every month on the 1st, once" there') — so an implementer who runs the suite and sees 'the 1st' recognises it as the pin rather than a bug, but it is written into no assertion.

I also fixed the asymmetry the objection pointed at inside risks[]. v4 treated the fixture date as unstable in one entry (status across midnight) while pinning the ordinal as stable in six others; the instability is in the string, not the status. The new risks[] keeps the midnight entry (it is genuinely about status) and states the new invariant instead: the trigger assertions compare two strings the app rendered, so they hold in any locale, and the only way they fail is if the start value changed between the two reads — which this change cannot cause.

The one judgement beyond the reviewer's instruction, disclosed here. The review offered two forms for AC-1/AC-2 and qa_script — derive from the pre-Apply text, or state it as a function of the run date. I took the first, but a QA agent working only from how_to_verify would otherwise still be invited to type a day, so AC-1's steps say explicitly to write the text down character for character and AC-2's say the same, with examples given as conditional ('e.g. ... on the 4th'). Offering a second way of saying the same thing would have reintroduced the exact ambiguity that sank v4.

Everything else carries forward from v4 unchanged in substance: the pre/post-Apply split (verified against RecurringSchedulePicker.tsx:632 and the single onSave write-back), the replaceModal fix, the console-guard narrowing, the edit-path coverage, the three page-model renames, the fixture restore, the release note, and finding 7's explicit instruction (leave getByRole('menu') unscoped) preferred over finding 4's, with the repo-wide pass left in out_of_scope. The five acceptance criteria are unchanged and each is either browser-observable or run by CI.
residual_risks: The exhausted-recurrence fixture is the ticket's load-bearing test and it is a long UI journey; a future change to the picker's layout or the RecurConfig shape breaks it in a way that reads as a test failure rather than a product one.

Comparing the pre- and post-Apply trigger strings means a copy edit or i18n change to the base description shows up only if it changes between the two reads — the desired sensitivity — but the assertion gives no diagnostic about which side moved. A future reader debugging it should compare the two captured strings rather than look for a literal.

Deleting the probe self-check leaves the two React warning literals unverified against a future React upgrade — they are React's own wording, and a constant declared beside the regex proves nothing about the app.

No CI job runs the e2e suite, so the claim that these tests fail without the fix is proven only by a local run. It is written into the tests[] cases and the last qa_script step, but no stage enforces it.

review.title: AC-4's automated guard only bites in a dev build. Under `E2E_USE_BUILD=1` — a supported path in playwright.config.ts:38-43 — `expect(messages).toEqual([])` passes vacuously, because React strips controlled/uncontrolled warnings from production bundles and the collector can then only ever be empty. Nothing in the test says which build it needs, so a regression that reintroduces the unguarded input still shows green on a production-build run.

Evidence: Removing the `|| ''` guard at ScheduleEditForm.tsx:134 and rebuilding with `yarn build:browser` leaves `-g "hides skip"` GREEN (1 passed, 8.8s) — the assertion passes because nothing is emitted, not because the warning is absent. This is likely caused by the value changing from undefined to a defined value…", so the collector is genuinely load-bearing. Scope note: the DEFAULT is safe — playwright.config.ts:38-43 runs `yarn start` unless `E2E_USE_BUILD` is set, and the work order's regression step uses `E2E_START_URL` against a manually started `yarn start`. Fix: Optional. Make the guard self-describing rather than environment-dependent: have the test assert it is on a dev build (skip-with-explanation, or fail fast) before asserting the collector is empty, so a production-build run reports "not verified" instead of "pass". At minimum a comment on `expect(messages).toEqual([])` naming the dev-build requirement would stop the next reader from trusting a green production run.

review.detail:
AC-4's console guard passes vacuously under `E2E_USE_BUILD=1`, because the production bundle strips React's controlled/uncontrolled warnings entirely, so the assertion can report green for a regression it cannot see. The test names no build requirement, so a reader has no way to tell a verified run from an unverifiable one.

`packages/desktop-client/e2e/schedules.test.ts:504`

Evidence: I reproduced this rather than inferring it. Removing the `|| ''` guard at ScheduleEditForm.tsx:134 and rebuilding with `yarn build:browser`: `grep -rl 'changing an uncontrolled input' packages/desktop-client/build/static/js/*.js` returns nothing (the string survives only in `.map` files), while `grep -rl 'recurrence-description' packages/desktop-client/build/static/js/` confirms the app code itself is in the bundle — the warnings are gone, not the app. Running the suite against that build with the guard still removed: `E2E_PORT=3011 E2E_USE_BUILD=1 playwright test schedules.test.ts -g 'hides skip'` → 1 passed. The same removal against the `yarn start` dev server → RED on `expect(messages).toEqual([])`, so the collector is genuinely load-bearing there. Scope, stated plainly: the default path is safe. playwright.config.ts:38-43 runs `yarn start` unless `E2E_USE_BUILD` is set, no workflow in `.github/workflows/` sets it, and AC-4's own how_to_verify already says to read the console on the dev server. This is a latent gap in a supported-but-unexercised configuration, not a live one.

Fix: Cheapest useful change: a comment on `expect(messages).toEqual([])` naming the dev-build requirement, so the next reader does not read a green production run as verification. Better: assert the build before asserting the collector — if `process.env.NODE_ENV` is not development in the page, skip with an explanation naming the dev-build requirement, so the run reports 'not verified' rather than 'pass'.
